articles.title: Kenneth Branagh on Doing His Own Stunts as a KGB Operative in ‘Mayday,’ Bonding With Ryan Reynolds Over Soccer: ‘We Can Be Pretty Nerdish’
articles.summary: While he may not be known as an action star, Kenneth Branagh absolutely wanted to give it a go for “Mayday,” his upcoming Apple TV Cold War action-comedy in which he co-stars with Ryan Reynolds. He just needed to find out how best to get involved. “I asked the directors, ‘What’s the way to do
body: “Mayday,” being released by Apple TV on Sept. 4, is set in the Soviet Union in 1987 and follows Reynolds’ crashed U.S. Air Force Pilot as he teams with Branagh’s former ex-KGB man — someone he describes as a “‘Top Gun’-loving exile in the forest of Siberia” — to escape.

While not throwing themselves around the snow in Canada, where the film mostly shot, Branagh and Reynolds bonded over a love of soccer, with Branagh being an avid lifetime supporter of Tottenham Hotspur and Reynolds as co-owner of Wrexham alongside Rob McElhenney.

“That was a source of, for me, fascination, at how they were living the dream,” said Branagh, who recalls the very first press conference when the new Wrexham co-owners said that they hoped to take the club from non-division football to the Premier League. “The snorts of derision were involuntary and fun, but now here they are in the Championship [the second tier below the Premier League]. Come on, this is quite something. So yes, we can be pretty nerdish about the beautiful game.”

articles.title: Canada’s H264 Nabs Colombia’s ‘Where the River Begins’ Ahead of Toronto Fest World Premiere
articles.summary: Canadian distributor h264 has pounced on worldwide sales rights to “Where the River Begins” (“Donde comienza el rio”) by Colombian-Canadian filmmaker Juan Andrés Arango (“La Playa DC”), ahead of its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival (TIFF).
body: Said h264 president Jean-Christophe Lamontagne: “’Where the River Begins” is a bold and deeply rooted film with the ability to resonate far beyond its place of origin. Juan Andrés Arango’s singular vision, combined with the strength of the project, makes us incredibly excited about the film’s international journey as we head into TIFF.”

“’Where the River Begins’ is a film about the universal search for a place we can call home, told from the singular perspective of a young Embera mother. For me, having this film selected for TIFF represents an ideal starting point for its international journey, at a festival renowned precisely for its great diversity of voices,” Arango told Variety.

articles.title: ‘Supporting Role’ Director Ana Urushadze Preps ‘Fear of Butterflies,’ a Detective Story With ‘Mysticism and a Touch of Body Horror’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Georgian director Ana Urushadze (“Scary Mother”), whose Rotterdam prizewinner “Supporting Role” plays in competition this week at the Sarajevo Film Festival, is prepping her third feature film.
body: It was an ah-ha moment for the director, an avowed hypochondriac. “Something clicked,” she said — although that hasn’t helped to conquer her phobia.

“Fear of Butterflies” will reunite Urushadze with Estonian producer Ivo Felt’s Tallinn-based shingle Allfilm, a co-producer on “Supporting Role.” With a bitter rift dividing the Georgian film industry, which has witnessed a long-running boycott by many directors, producers, actors and other industry professionals against the state-backed Georgian National Film Center, the director said she’s looking abroad for financing — and isn’t even certain if the film will be made in Georgia. “I’m really open to anything,” she said.

It is a bittersweet prospect for Urushadze, whose much-feted feature debut “Scary Mother,” which won the prize for best first feature at Locarno in 2017 as well as the top honors in Sarajevo, was described by Variety ’s Jessica Kiang as “a startling debut that wholly earns its place as standard-bearer for one of the most exciting and distinctive national cinemas to have emerged in recent years.”

articles.title: Spa Weekend review – female answer to The Hangover spreads the slush with the massage oil
articles.summary: Despite stars Leslie Mann, Anna Faris and Isla Fisher and the writers behind The Hangover, this tale of friends at a luxury hotel is a dud. Jon Lucas and Scott Moore are the screenwriters who struck gold nearly 20 years ago with The Hangover, a brilliant stag-weekend nightmare comedy about what…
body: Leslie Mann plays a hotshot lawyer called Jane who can’t make room in her life for romance; Anna Faris is goofy Sophie, PA to a rich asshole; Michelle Buteau is outspoken badass Coco, angry at her ex-husband dating again; and Isla Fisher is landed with the stridently unfunny role of Mel, a wild child who makes the other three nervous, but whose life-affirming no-filter honesty is going to break everyone’s emotional logjam and sort out their lives. As for Jane, it looks as if the hotel’s super-hot super-sensitive yoga teacher, Kai (Adam Demos), is going to hook up with her.

The potentially funny idea of the one woman in the friend group whom no one really likes might have been the grit in the oyster that produced the comedy pearl, but, of course, it has to turn out that they really do like Mel – and in a much slushier, more sentimental way than the guys in The Hangover came round to liking Zach Galifianakis’s character. There’s something bland in this movie’s massage oil.

articles.title: Starmer donates biography of himself to Downing Street library
articles.summary: The former PM and seven of his ministers have added to the collection, which began in 1931.
body: A book about the life of Sir Keir Starmer has become the newest addition to the Downing Street library, after being donated by Sir Keir himself.

Keir Starmer: The Biography, written by journalist and former Labour adviser Tom Baldwin, has now joined the collection of more than 400 books, some of which are kept in two bookcases in Downing Street's Cabinet Room.
The library was established in 1931 by the first Labour Prime Minister, Ramsay MacDonald, and since then prime ministers and ministers have been invited to make contributions.
Seven ministers who served in Sir Keir's government have also added books to the shelves.

articles.title: ‘It is the riskiest film I’ve ever made’: Pedro Almodóvar on being the villain in his own movie
articles.summary: As his new film Bitter Christmas is released, the legendary Spanish director turns his fire on Donald Trump, Will Smith, Netflix – and himself. Black sunglasses indoors and a tufty cloud of cotton-wool hair: it can only be Pedro Almodóvar, bourgeois arthouse darling nonpareil and master of…
body: Then again, mixing contradictory flavours is part of what he does. There is the blank, blase approach to extreme material (murder, paedophilia, telekinesis) in his 1984 comedy What Have I Done to Deserve This? Or the climax of Matador, his kinky 1986 thriller, in which the race to prevent a double murder is paused while the characters gawp at a solar eclipse. A rape scene becomes comic in Kika, from 1993, and another rape is euphemised as a silent movie pastiche in 2002’s Oscar-winning Talk to Her.

Keeping track of what is happening on screen becomes a case of mind over meta. Why should we care about Elsa’s story, though, when it is merely the product of Raúl’s imagination? “I hope that when the audience discovers that the film-within-a-film is going to change, that this change will surprise and excite them. But you’re right, it’s very risky. I think it is the riskiest film I’ve ever made. I took a whole bunch of risks, even knowing that some might not land. It requires you to pay complete attention, and it does seem to me that film audiences are increasingly getting lazy.”

body: Actor Dave Bautista has been cast in the lead role of the upcoming God of War TV show.
The ex-WWE star will play Kratos in the adaptation of the PlayStation video game series, after Ryan Hurst was forced to quit the part due to injury.
Bautista, who had been rumoured to be in line to take the part for weeks, confirmed the casting by posting an image of the character to his Instagram account.

articles.title: British rapper Yung Filly to face retrial on rape charges in Australia
articles.summary: A jury last month cleared the YouTuber of several sexual assault offences, but it couldn't reach a decision on three others.
body: British rapper Yung Filly will face a retrial on three rape charges in Australia, after a jury cleared him of several sexual assault offences but could not reach a decision on others.
The YouTuber, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, was charged with repeatedly raping and assaulting a fan after performing at a nightclub in Perth in 2024.
He denied all 10 charges, and last month a jury found him not guilty on three counts of rape.
He was also acquitted of one assault charge and another of strangulation, but was found guilty of two counts of assault, for which he will be sentenced after his retrial.

articles.title: It Ends Review: An Endless Road Trip That Evolves Into An Existential Nightmare
articles.summary: Alexander Ullom's feature directorial debut, It Ends, is a strong cap to a powerhouse summer for first-time horror filmmakers. Here's our review.
body: From the outset of this realization (with hordes of screaming people sprinting out of the woods, desperately clawing to get into their car), "It Ends" has all the makings of a survival horror thriller. But when the drive continues on, and on, and on, Ullom's film reveals itself to be something far more interesting.

When leaving my press screening of the film, I overheard some colleagues older than me (I'm 36) lament that they found it "boring" and "lacking anything important to say." When asked for my thoughts, I reflexively responded in the most self-deprecating Millennial fashion possible and practically choked on my confession of, "This movie made me want to kill myself and then not kill myself, I loved it."

"It Ends" is ordinary right up until it isn't, and that's the great magic trick of Alexander Ullom's debut. The horror is found in questioning our understanding of who we are as we navigate life without knowing where we're going. The endless road — scattered with cars that have maxed out their odometers and forests of people at varying degrees of acceptance — is a conceit that provides a simple thought experiment with compelling execution.
points: Alexander Ullom's feature directorial debut, It Ends, is a strong cap to a powerhouse summer for first-time horror filmmakers.
